## Question 1

### Part a
#### 1

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(354)

R <- 1000
simulations <- vector("list", R)

for (i in 1:R) {
  simulations[[i]] <- data.frame(
    value = rnorm(150, mean = 0, sd = 1),
    group = factor(rep(1:5, each = 30))
  )
}
```
:::


#### 2

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
error_unadjusted <- logical(R)

for (i in 1:R) {
  dat <- simulations[[i]]

  test_unadjusted <- pairwise.t.test(
    dat$value, dat$group,
    p.adjust.method = "none"
  )

  error_unadjusted[i] <- any(
    test_unadjusted$p.value < 0.05,
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
}

mean(error_unadjusted)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.294
```


:::
:::


At least one pairwise comparison provided statistically discernible
support for a non-zero mean difference in
294 of the 1,000 simulations (p < 0.05).
These are Type I errors,
giving an estimated family-wise error rate of
29.4%.

#### 3


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
error_tukey <- logical(R)

for (i in 1:R) {
  dat <- simulations[[i]]

  fit <- aov(value ~ group, data = dat)
  test_tukey <- rstatix::tukey_hsd(fit)

  error_tukey[i] <- any(test_tukey$p.adj < 0.05)
}

mean(error_tukey)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.053
```


:::
:::


After Tukey's HSD adjustment, at least one pairwise comparison
provided statistically discernible support for a non-zero mean
difference in 53 of the 1,000 simulations
(adjusted p < 0.05).
Since all population means were zero, these are Type I errors,
and the estimated family-wise error rate is
5.3%.


### Part b


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
error_bh <- logical(R)

for (i in 1:R) {
  dat <- simulations[[i]]

  test_bh <- pairwise.t.test(
    dat$value, dat$group,
    p.adjust.method = "BH"
  )

  error_bh[i] <- any(
    test_bh$p.value < 0.05,
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
}

mean(error_bh)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.047
```


:::
:::


After BH adjustment, at least one pairwise comparison provided
statistically discernible support for a non-zero mean difference
in 47 of the 1,000 simulations, giving an estimated
family-wise error rate of 4.7%.
This was much lower than the unadjusted rate of
29.4% and close to Tukey's
rate of 5.3%.

BH targets the false discovery rate (FDR), whereas Tukey's HSD
controls the family-wise error rate (FWER). 

## Question 2

### Part a


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Required sample size per group
pwr::pwr.anova.test(
  k = 5,
  f = 0.25,
  sig.level = 0.05,
  power = 0.80
)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

     Balanced one-way analysis of variance power calculation 

              k = 5
              n = 39.1534
              f = 0.25
      sig.level = 0.05
          power = 0.8

NOTE: n is number in each group
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Power curve
n <- 2:100

power <- sapply(n, function(x) {
  pwr::pwr.anova.test(
    k = 5, n = x, f = 0.25, sig.level = 0.05
  )$power
})

plot(n, power, type = "l",
     xlab = "Sample size per group",
     ylab = "Power",
     main = "ANOVA Power Curve")

abline(h = 0.80, col = "red", lty = 2)
abline(v = 40, col = "blue", lty = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](HW2_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-5-1.pdf){fig-pos='H'}
:::
:::


The required sample size is roughly 40 participants per group and 200 in total.
The graph shows that 40 participants per group achieves slightly
more than 80% power.

Since every group in the original groups had more than 40
participants, the study is powered for the overall
ANOVA under the assumed moderate effect size. This calculation
assumes equal group sizes, so it does not provide the exact power
of the original unequal-sized design.


### Part b


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Non-centrality parameter and power
lambda <- 150 * 0.25^2
lambda
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 9.375
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
critical <- qf(0.95, 4, 145)
pf(critical, 4, 145, ncp = lambda, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.6675964
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Alternative F distribution
curve(df(x, 4, 145, ncp = lambda), from = 0, to = 10,
      xlab = "F", ylab = "Density",
      main = "Alternative F Distribution: N = 150")
abline(v = critical, col = "red", lty = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](HW2_files/figure-pdf/unnamed-chunk-6-1.pdf){fig-pos='H'}
:::
:::


With 30 participants per group, the non-centrality parameter is
9.375 and the power is approximately 66.8%. Therefore, N = 150
is insufficient to achieve the desired 80% power.

### Part c


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Power for different sample sizes per group
n <- 40:500

power_c <- sapply(n, function(x) {
  PMCMRplus::power.tukey.test(
    n = x,
    groups = 5,
    delta = 0.25,
    within.var = 0.7152,
    sig.level = 0.05
  )$power
})

# Power with 40 participants per group
power_c[1]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.07866837
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Smallest sample size achieving at least 80% power
n_required <- min(n[power_c >= 0.80])
n_required
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 293
```


:::
:::


An overall ANOVA can detect differences among groups having different
means. However, detecting the smaller difference between
stages 1 and 2 is harder, especially after Tukey's adjustment
for multiple comparisons.

    design = "5b",
    n = n,

    nsims = 1000,
    seed = 354,
    emm = TRUE,
    emm_p_adjust = "tukey",
    verbose = FALSE

  print(paste("Sample size per group:", n))
  print(result$main_result)
  print(result$emm_results)
}
